title: Unit finale: window and deque
sub: New problems, a Minimum Window Substring trace with repeats in t, a trap and explaining out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match each statement with its technique.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: The longest run of ones if you may flip at most k zeros
cards/0/pairs/0/1: Variable-size window: zeros in the window ≤ k
cards/0/pairs/1/0: Every position in s where a permutation of p starts
cards/0/pairs/1/1: A window of length |p| and letter counters
cards/0/pairs/2/0: How many subarrays sum to exactly k, numbers of any sign
cards/0/pairs/3/0: The minimum of every window of k elements
cards/0/pairs/4/0: The largest sum of k consecutive numbers
cards/0/pairs/4/1: Fixed-size window: + the incoming, − the leaving
cards/1/q: Max Consecutive Ones III (LeetCode #1004): an array of 0s and 1s, you may flip at most k zeros; find the longest run of ones. What do you keep in the window and when do you shrink?
cards/1/options/0: A count of zeros in the window; shrink from the left while there are more than k zeros
cards/1/options/1: A count of ones in the window; shrink while there are fewer than k ones
cards/1/options/2: A window does not fit: you need prefix sums
cards/1/explain: A window is valid if its zeros can be flipped: zeros ≤ k. The condition is monotonic — a valid window’s sub-windows have no more zeros — so the “longest” template works: grow on the right, shrink while the window is bad, take the answer after the while. It is #424 with budget k, except the “extra” letters are always zeros. O(n), O(1) memory.
cards/1/wrong/1: Ones cost nothing — the budget is spent on zeros. The window is bad when there are more than k zeros.
cards/1/wrong/2: There are no negative numbers here, and “zeros ≤ k” is monotonic. Prefixes are needed when monotonicity breaks.
cards/2/q: The shortest subarray with sum ≥ k, numbers from −10⁵ to 10⁵, n ≤ 10⁵. What do you choose?
cards/2/options/0: Prefix sums and a monotonic deque of indices
cards/2/options/1: A variable-size window: shrink while the sum is ≥ k
cards/2/options/2: A fixed-size window for every length from 1 to n
cards/2/explain: Negative numbers break monotonicity: shrinking can increase the sum, and the window misses the answer — as on [1, −1, 5] with target 5. This is LeetCode #862: prefixes plus a deque of indices with increasing prefixes, O(n). Trying every length is O(n²), which is 10¹⁰ for 10⁵.
cards/2/wrong/1: On [1, −1, 5], target 5, the window returns 3, but the answer is 1: reaching [5] requires dropping the −1, which would increase the sum.
cards/2/wrong/2: It works, but it is O(n²): n lengths of n steps each. For n = 10⁵ that is 10¹⁰ operations.
cards/3/task: Step through the Minimum Window Substring trace on s = "BAXAYBAA", t = "AAB" — t has two As. The rig asks twice what happens to the formed counter.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: need = {A: 2, B: 1}, need.Count = 2. The window is “B”, formed = 1. The first “A” arrives. What does formed become?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: have[A] = 1, but 2 are needed: the letter A is not covered yet, so formed stays 1. formed grows only at the moment have[c] becomes exactly need[c] — for A that happens on the second “A”.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Drops the “A” — coverage is lost, formed = 1
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Drops the “A”, coverage holds: there is another A in the window
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Records “AYBA” as the new best window
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: The window “AYBA” covers t, and an “A” is on the left. The best so far is “BAXA”. What does the code do?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: “AYBA” has length 4 — no shorter than “BAXA”, so the record stays (it must be strictly less). The “A” leaves: have[A] drops from 2 to 1 < 2, the letter A becomes uncovered, formed = 1. One A is still in the window, but two are needed. Then another “A” arrives, and the window shrinks to the answer “BAA”.
cards/4/q: On the string "abcbd" this code returns 4, but the right answer is 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: At r = 3 a “b” arrives at the window “abc”. The if removes only the “a”, l = 1, while the first “b” stays; Add of the second “b” returns false. The window “bcb”, which has a repeat, counts as valid, and at r = 4 “bcbd” gives 4. Shrink while the duplicate is inside: a while, not an if.
cards/5/q: Window maximum, k = 3, nums = [6, 2, 5, 3, 4]. After i = 3 the deque holds indices [2, 3] — values 5, 3. i = 4, x = 4 arrives. What is in the deque after the step, and what is the window maximum?
cards/5/explain: The front: index 2 ≤ 4 − 3 = 1? No — the 5 is still in the window [2..4]. The back: 3 ≤ 4 — pop it; 5 ≤ 4 — no, stop. Push 4. The deque is [2, 4], the values decrease, and the maximum is the front, 5.
cards/5/wrong/1: The 5 at index 2 is still in the window [2..4]: only an index ≤ i − k = 1 leaves from the front. And only those ≤ x leave from the back.
cards/5/wrong/2: The 3 is ≤ 4 and to its left — it will never be the maximum again, so it is popped. Otherwise the deque values would stop decreasing.
cards/5/wrong/3: The 5 is greater than the 4 — it is not popped from the back, and it has not left the window.
cards/6/q: The complexity of this unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/6/options/0: A variable-size window with a while inside a for is O(n) because l only grows
cards/6/options/2: A monotonic deque for the window maximum is O(n): every index enters and leaves once
cards/6/options/3: The honest #424 that recomputes the maximum over 26 counters is O(26·n)
cards/6/options/4: A SortedSet for the window maximum is O(n) because Max takes O(1)
cards/6/explain: A nested while does not make the window quadratic: l moves at most n times per pass. Minimum Window is O(|s| + |t|): t is counted once and formed is checked in O(1). The deque is ≤ 2n operations. The honest #424 is 26 operations per step. A SortedSet is O(n log k): insertion and removal in the tree are O(log k), and Max also walks to the rightmost node.
cards/7/q: Unity: the HUD needs the worst frame over the last 120 frames. What is the sensible choice?
cards/7/options/0: Scan the ring buffer of 120 values every frame: 120 comparisons take microseconds
cards/7/options/1: A monotonic deque only: otherwise it is O(n·k) and the game will stutter
cards/7/options/2: A SortedSet of frame times with removal of the leaving one
cards/7/explain: k = 120 and one window per frame: a plain scan costs microseconds, with no allocations and no chance of a bug. “O(n·k)” here means 120 operations per frame, not per game. A deque pays off when the window and the stream are large. A SortedSet allocates a tree node on every insertion — garbage every frame.
cards/7/wrong/1: There is one window per frame, and scanning it is 120 comparisons. Asymptotics matter when k and n are large; here the constant is tiny.
cards/7/wrong/2: It works, but every insertion into a SortedSet is a new heap node, which is GC garbage every frame. And it is more complex than a plain scan.
cards/8/q: You are solving Max Consecutive Ones III out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/8/items/0: Clarify: the array holds only 0s and 1s, k can be 0, n up to 10⁵
cards/8/items/1: Name the brute force: every subarray with a count of zeros — O(n²)
cards/8/items/2: Recognise the pattern: the longest subarray with the monotonic condition “zeros ≤ k” — a variable-size window
cards/8/items/3: Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: after the while there are at most k zeros in the window
cards/8/items/4: Run [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1], k = 2 and show where the window shrinks
cards/8/items/5: State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory — l only grows
cards/8/items/6: Edge cases: k = 0, all zeros, all ones, k ≥ the number of zeros
cards/8/explain: The same script as in every lesson of the unit: the statement, the baseline, the pattern from its signals (a contiguous piece, “the longest”, a monotonic condition), code with the invariant, a run, the complexity, edge cases. With k ≥ the number of zeros the answer is n, and the code should produce it on its own, with no special case.
